L24: # GetWindowTextW function (winuser.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Copies the text of the specified window's title bar (if it has one) into a buffer. If the specified window is a control, the text of the control is copied. However, GetWindowText cannot retrieve the text of a control in another application.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `int GetWindowTextW(
L37:       [in]  HWND   hWnd,
L38:       [out] LPWSTR lpString,
L39:       [in]  int    nMaxCount
L40:     );
L41:     `
L42: ## Parameters
L43: 
L44: `[in] hWnd`
L45: 
L46: Type: HWND
L47: 
L48: A handle to the window or control containing the text.
L49: 
L50: `[out] lpString`
L51: 
L52: Type: LPTSTR
L53: 
L54: The buffer that will receive the text. If the string is as long or longer than the buffer, the string is truncated and terminated with a null character.
L55: 
L56: `[in] nMaxCount`
L57: 
L58: Type: int
L59: 
L60: The maximum number of characters to copy to the buffer, including the null character. If the text exceeds this limit, it is truncated.
L61: ## Return value
L62: 
L63: Type: int
L64: 
L65: If the function succeeds, the return value is the length, in characters, of the copied string, not including the terminating null character. If the window has no title bar or text, if the title bar is empty, or if the window or control handle is invalid, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call cite5†GetLastError .
L66: 
L67: This function cannot retrieve the text of an edit control in another application.
L68: ## Remarks
L69: If the target window is owned by the current process, GetWindowText causes a cite6†WM_GETTEXT message to be sent to the specified window or control. If the target window is owned by another process and has a caption, GetWindowText retrieves the window caption text. If the window does not have a caption, the return value is a null string. This behavior is by design. It allows applications to call GetWindowText without becoming unresponsive if the process that owns the target window is not responding.
L70: However, if the target window is not responding and it belongs to the calling application, GetWindowText will cause the calling application to become unresponsive.
L71: To retrieve the text of a control in another process, send a cite6†WM_GETTEXT message directly instead of calling GetWindowText.
L72: #### Examples
L73: 
L74: For an example, see cite7†Sending a Message .
L75: 
L76: Note
L77: 
L78: The winuser.h header defines GetWindowText as an alias that automatically selects the ANSI or Unicode version of this function based on the definition of the UNICODE preprocessor constant. Mixing usage of the encoding-neutral alias with code that is not encoding-neutral can lead to mismatches that result in compilation or runtime errors. For more information, see cite8†Conventions for Function Prototypes .

L24: # SendMessageTimeoutW function (winuser.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Sends the specified message to one or more windows.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `LRESULT SendMessageTimeoutW(
L37:       [in]            HWND       hWnd,
L38:       [in]            UINT       Msg,
L39:       [in]            WPARAM     wParam,
L40:       [in]            LPARAM     lParam,
L41:       [in]            UINT       fuFlags,
L42:       [in]            UINT       uTimeout,
L43:       [out, optional] PDWORD_PTR lpdwResult
L44:     );
L45:     `
L46: ## Parameters
L47: 
L48: `[in] hWnd`
L49: 
L50: Type: HWND
L51: 
L52: A handle to the window whose window procedure will receive the message.
L53: 
L54: If this parameter is HWND_BROADCAST ((HWND)0xffff), the message is sent to all top-level windows in the system, including disabled or invisible unowned windows. The function does not return until each window has timed out. Therefore, the total wait time can be up to the value of uTimeout multiplied by the number of top-level windows.
L55: 
L56: `[in] Msg`
L57: 
L58: Type: UINT
L59: 
L60: The message to be sent.
L61: For lists of the system-provided messages, see cite5†System-Defined Messages .
L62: 
L63: `[in] wParam`
L64: 
L65: Type: WPARAM
L66: 
L67: Any additional message-specific information.
L68: 
L69: `[in] lParam`
L70: 
L71: Type: LPARAM
L72: 
L73: Any additional message-specific information.
L74: 
L75: `[in] fuFlags`
L76: 
L77: Type: UINT
L78: 
L79: The behavior of this function. This parameter can be one or more of the following values.
L80: 
L81: Value  | Meaning
L82: --- | ---
L83: SMTO_ABORTIFHUNG
L84: 0x0002
L85:  | The function returns without waiting for the time-out period to elapse if the receiving thread appears to not respond or "hangs."
L86: 
L87: SMTO_BLOCK
L88: 0x0001
L89:  | Prevents the calling thread from processing any other requests until the function returns.
L90: 
L91: SMTO_NORMAL
L92: 0x0000
L93:  | The calling thread is not prevented from processing other requests while waiting for the function to return.
L94: SMTO_NOTIMEOUTIFNOTHUNG
L95: 0x0008
L96:  | The function does not enforce the time-out period as long as the receiving thread is processing messages.
L97: 
L98: SMTO_ERRORONEXIT
L99: 0x0020
L100:  | The function should return 0 if the receiving window is destroyed or its owning thread dies while the message is being processed.
L101: 
L102: `[in] uTimeout`
L103: 
L104: Type: UINT
L105: The duration of the time-out period, in milliseconds. If the message is a broadcast message, each window can use the full time-out period. For example, if you specify a five second time-out period and there are three top-level windows that fail to process the message, you could have up to a 15 second delay.
L106: 
L107: `[out, optional] lpdwResult`
L108: 
L109: Type: PDWORD_PTR
L110: 
L111: The result of the message processing. The value of this parameter depends on the message that is specified.
L112: ## Return value
L113: 
L114: Type: LRESULT
L115: 
L116: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero. SendMessageTimeout does not provide information about individual windows timing out if HWND_BROADCAST is used.
L117: If the function fails or times out, the return value is 0. Note that the function does not always call cite6†SetLastError on failure. If the reason for failure is important to you, call SetLastError(ERROR_SUCCESS) before calling SendMessageTimeout. If the function returns 0, and cite7†GetLastError returns ERROR_SUCCESS, then treat it as a generic failure.
L118: ## Remarks
L119: 
L120: The function calls the window procedure for the specified window and, if the specified window belongs to a different thread, does not return until the window procedure has processed the message or the specified time-out period has elapsed. If the window receiving the message belongs to the same queue as the current thread, the window procedure is called directly—the time-out value is ignored.
L121: This function considers that a thread is not responding if it has not called cite8†GetMessage or a similar function within five seconds.

L123: The system only does marshalling for system messages (those in the range 0 to (cite9†WM_USER -1)). To send other messages (those >= WM_USER) to another process, you must do custom marshalling.
